title: Paul's journeys
hookLine: many miles on foot and by sea, making tents to pay his way
last: IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE SPIRIT AND US.

cards: A workshop in Corinth. Needles, heavy thread, rough material pinned across a bench, and three people working it: a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, and a traveler just arrived from Athens.
Acts says it simply: "because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers." The traveler is Paul.
His road fills the later chapters of Acts, and on a weekday in Corinth he is sewing tents to pay his way.

teach.b: Acts follows Paul out of Antioch with Barnabas, across the sea to Cyprus and up into the hill towns of Asia Minor. Later, in Troas on the coast, he sees a man in a night vision: "Come over into Macedonia, and help us."
So he crosses into Europe. In Philippi a businesswoman named Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, opens her home to the new church. Then Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus.
Readers draw them as journeys on maps in the back of their Bibles, but Acts tells it as one long road. A hard one.

Paul lists it himself, writing to Corinth: "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers."
So why work at all? He tells the Thessalonians: "labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you." He didn't want the message to come with a bill.

To the elders of Ephesus he holds up his hands: "these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me." His friends' needs too. So the picture of Paul isn't only the preacher in the marketplace.
It's the man at the bench with a needle, who also "reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath." Some Christians who work ordinary jobs while serving a church call themselves tentmakers, after him.

how: Christians read Paul's journeys in Acts and in his letters, often with the maps printed in the back of some Bibles, and people who serve a church while working an ordinary job are sometimes called tentmakers after him.

practice: If you have a phone or an atlas handy, find Antioch in the corner where Turkey meets Syria, then Cyprus, Philippi in northern Greece, Athens and Corinth to the south, and Ephesus across the water, tracing the line slowly with a finger.
If you can't look at a map, walk it in your mind: a coast, a ship, a dusty road, a workshop. If you pray, pray for someone traveling today.

wordCard.voice: Paul's journeys. The roads and sea crossings Acts follows, from Antioch to Europe and back, paid for by a tentmaker's hands.
